title: Closing the Loop: Learning to Generate Writing Feedback via Language Model Simulated Student Revisions
extended_summary:
This paper addresses how to train a language-model-based writing feedback generator so that the feedback it produces is more effective for improving student revisions. The authors argue that although large language models can generate actionable comments, it is difficult to specify in advance which feedback attributes actually lead to better revision outcomes. They therefore propose optimizing a feedback generator directly against revision quality, using simulated student revisions rather than repeated testing with real students.

The intervention studied is PROF, a method that trains a feedback generation model by iteratively sampling multiple candidate feedback comments for a student essay, using a language-model student simulator to generate revised essays from each candidate, scoring those revisions with GPT-4 using the course rubric, and then using preference optimization to update the feedback generator. The study also analyzes two student simulators (Llama3-8B- and GPT-3.5-based) and compares PROF against several baselines, including few-shot GPT-3.5, few-shot GPT-4, and a supervised fine-tuned model trained on human peer feedback. Outcomes are primarily intrinsic pedagogical quality of generated feedback and extrinsic simulated revision quality.

The population and context are undergraduate students in Economics 101 at the University of Michigan, Ann Arbor, in the United States. The assignment asked students to write a persuasive economics letter about minimum wage increases and automation policy in San Francisco. The dataset contained 363 submission datapoints consisting of an initial essay, three peer reviews, and a revised essay. This is not a direct secondary-school comparative trial of ChatGPT feedback versus teacher or peer feedback; instead, it is a university-based modeling study using existing student writing and peer feedback data.

The main conclusions are that PROF improves over the supervised fine-tuned feedback generator and can match or exceed enterprise LLM baselines on simulated revision effectiveness while also showing competitive pedagogical alignment. The authors conclude that LM-simulated student revisions can be useful for training and evaluating feedback generators, but they also note that findings are limited by the narrow domain and by reliance on LLM-based simulation and scoring rather than direct classroom outcome testing with real learners.
quality_tier_rationale: This is not eligible K-12 evidence for the requested topic: the study is in a U.S. university introductory economics course, not grades 9-12, and it does not directly compare ChatGPT feedback against teacher, peer, or no-feedback conditions in real secondary students. Outcomes are largely based on LM-simulated revisions and LLM judging rather than direct causal student evidence.
impact_tier_rationale: The paper shows promising but unclear impact on writing revision quality within a simulated university setting, with no directly reported effect sizes and no direct secondary-school student outcome evidence. For the requested K-12 feedback-only evidence base, direct impact is effectively absent.

interventions.use_case: LLM-based automated generation of formative feedback on university students' economics essays, optimized using simulated student revisions to improve revision implementation quality.
Use of GPT-3.5/GPT-4 and fine-tuned LLaMA models as essay feedback and scoring tools for generating peer-review-style comments and rubric-based evaluation of revised essays.

finding.finding_summary: In a university economics essay task, the proposed PROF automated feedback system outperformed GPT-3.5/GPT-4 few-shot feedback baselines and generally matched or exceeded a supervised fine-tuned human-feedback baseline on extrinsic revision-quality scores generated by a GPT-3.5 student simulator. Average normalized revised-essay quality scores were 79.9 for PROF (tau=0.7, iteration 1) and 80.0 for PROF (tau=0.85, iteration 1), versus 76.8 for GPT-3.5, 77.0 for GPT-4, and 79.4 for the supervised baseline; however, these are simulator-judged outcomes rather than direct student post-feedback writing outcomes.
finding.measure: Normalized rubric-based essay quality of simulated revised essays in an economics writing assignment; intrinsic pedagogical feedback quality metrics included respects guided questions, encourages active learning, deepens metacognition, and motivates/stimulates curiosity.

finding.finding_summary: The paper reports improved pedagogical alignment of generated feedback, including stronger scores on dimensions linked to metacognition and active learning, with PROF approaching GPT-4 performance on average pedagogical quality. However, these are LLM-judged feedback-quality indicators rather than direct student measures of metacognition, self-regulation, or revision strategy, so evidence for durable-skill improvement is indirect.
finding.measure: LLM-judged pedagogical feedback dimensions: encourages active learning, deepens metacognition, respects guided questions, and motivates/stimulates student curiosity.
finding.study_size: 21 essay-review pairs for human-vs-GPT-4 validation of pedagogical scoring; main dataset n=363 datapoints
